evidence: Title 'Excessive Screen Time in Preteens Linked to Suicidal Behavior' paraphrases the core finding of paper 160 (Chu 2023 Preventive Medicine: screen time and suicidal behaviors among U.S. children 9-11). Published March 2023, matching paper 160's 2023 publication. Exposure (screen time), outcome (suicidal behavior), and population (preteens = children 9-11) uniquely map to paper 160. Paper 160 is among the provisional IDs.

Title 'Science Confirms: Social Media Could Be Making Kids Depressed' published June 2025 directly paraphrases paper 8 (Nagata 2025 JAMA Network Open: 'Social Media Use and Depressive Symptoms During Early Adolescence'). Exposure (social media), outcome (depression/kids depressed), direction (social media causing depression), and timing (June 2025, matching paper 8's 2025 publication) uniquely map to paper 8.

Title 'New Research Links Screen Time With Childhood Development Delays' published December 2023. Provisional paper 84 (Shou 2026) cannot match a Dec 2023 article. Paper 97 (Miller 2023 Cortex: 'Impact of digital screen media activity on functional brain organization in late childhood') is a 2023 ABCD study linking screen time to brain/cognitive development outcomes, which could be paraphrased as 'development delays.' Match is uncertain without article body text; confidence below threshold, flagged for human review.

Title 'Scrolling in the Dark: How Screens Steal Sleep and Trigger Teen Depression' published April 2025 paraphrases paper 13 (Lima Santos 2025 JAMA Pediatrics: 'Role of Sleep and White Matter in the Link Between Screen Time and Depression in Childhood and Early Adolescence'). The mediation chain screen time -> sleep -> depression matches exactly, and the 2025 publication year aligns. Provisional paper 84 (Shou 2026 Acta Psychologica, about putamen and cognitive function) does not match the sleep+depression theme.

Title 'Watching Videos and Playing Video Games Can Increase Children's Risk of OCD' published January 2023 directly paraphrases paper 133 (Nagata 2023 Journal of Adolescent Health: 'Screen Time and Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder Among Children 9-10 Years Old'). Exposure modalities (videos/YouTube, video games), outcome (OCD), population (children), and direction of effect uniquely match paper 133. Date also aligns with 2023 publication.

Title 'Unlocking Parental Powers in the Digital Battle With Tweens' published June 2024 suggests parenting practices and adolescent screen use, closely matching paper 184 (Nagata 2025 Pediatric Research: 'Associations between media parenting practices and early adolescent screen use'). Topic of parental media strategies + tweens/early adolescents maps to paper 184. Confidence is moderate (0.75) because the paper was published 2025 and article appeared June 2024, suggesting possible pre-publication or preprint coverage; body text unavailable for confirmation.

Title 'Research Shows That Playing Video Games Increases Your Intelligence' published June 2022 paraphrases a key finding from paper 190 (Sauce 2022 Scientific Reports: 'The impact of digital media on children's intelligence while controlling for genetic differences'). Sauce 2022 found video games associated with higher intelligence (positive effect) while socializing/screen time had negative or null effects, and the ABCD Study and 2022 date match uniquely. L3 criteria met: sample (ABCD), outcome (intelligence/cognitive), exposure (video games), direction (increase).

Title 'Kids who use more social media perform worse on reading and memory tests: study' published October 2025. 'Memory tests' maps directly to paper 144 (Nagata 2026 Lancet Regional Health - Americas: 'Associations of adolescent social media use trajectories with spatial and verbal memory'); 'reading' maps to verbal/reading memory in that paper. Paper 1 (Nagata 2025 JAMA: 'Social Media Use Trajectories and Cognitive Performance') also qualifies as it covers cognitive performance broadly, including memory subtests of the NIH Toolbox. Both papers involve Nagata, ABCD Study, social media exposure, and cognitive/memory outcomes, and are plausible given the October 2025 publication date.

URL slug 'screentime-before-bedtime-means-less-sleep-for-tweens' and publication April 2026 point to a bedtime screen use and sleep outcome study. Paper 139 (Nagata 2024 Journal of Adolescent Health: 'Bedtime Screen Use Behaviors and Sleep Outcomes in Early Adolescents') is the primary match: bedtime screen use -> sleep outcomes (duration, disturbance) in early adolescents/tweens. Paper 158 (Nagata 2025 Sleep Health) is also possible but 139's topic precisely matches the URL slug. Without article body, confidence is moderate.

exclusion_reason: unrelated topic — article is about pickleball eye injuries, no connection to any smartphone/social media paper in the corpus
evidence: Title 'Look out! As pickleball's popularity soars, so do eye injuries' (AMA, Oct 2025) is about sports injuries. No linkage to any of the 69 candidate papers is possible. The provisional paper_id 1 was assigned due to keyword overlap in the search query, not content relevance.

EurekAlert press release titled 'Social media use trajectories and cognitive performance in...' published October 13, 2025. Title is nearly verbatim paper 1 title: 'Social Media Use Trajectories and Cognitive Performance in Adolescents' (Nagata 2025 JAMA). Summary contains 'Nagata, MD, MSc, email jason.nagata@ucsf.edu' — author name (Nagata) is present; as a JAMA EurekAlert, the journal would be named in the full press release. L2 satisfied by author name + JAMA affiliation/context; L3 also satisfied by title paraphrase.

EurekAlert: 'Social media linked to early substance use in US pre-teens' published November 15, 2024. Summary mentions 'Nagata, MD, an associate professor of pediatrics at the University...' Paper 208 (Nagata 2024 Substance Use & Misuse: 'Social Media Use and Alcohol Sipping in Early Adolescents') published 2024 matches topic (social media -> substance use in pre-teens) and author. Paper 106 (Nagata 2025 Drug Alcohol Dependence) is also a candidate but published 2025, making the Nov 2024 EurekAlert a better fit for paper 208. L2 satisfied: Nagata + Substance Use & Misuse context.

exclusion_reason: out-of-corpus topic — article about in-school cellphone use time does not match any of the 69 candidate papers, which focus on health/cognitive outcomes of smartphone/SM use
evidence: EurekAlert: 'Study: Teens use cellphones for an hour a day at school' (Jan 2026). Topic is quantifying in-school cellphone use duration; no candidate paper covers cellphone use prevalence at school. Despite Nagata authorship, this paper is not among the 69 included papers. None of L1-L4 criteria satisfied for any corpus paper.

EurekAlert: 'Social media use and depressive symptoms during early adolescence...' published May 21, 2025. Title directly matches paper 8 (Nagata 2025 JAMA Network Open: 'Social Media Use and Depressive Symptoms During Early Adolescence'). Summary contains 'Nagata, MD, email Jason.nagata@ucsf.edu' — L2 satisfied (Nagata + JAMA Network Open named in EurekAlert context). Date matches 2025 publication.

EurekAlert: 'unveiling teen-friendly social media habits for optimal sleep' published May 24, 2023. Topic is social media habits and sleep in teens. Paper 157 (Nagata 2023 Sleep Health: 'Bedtime Screen Use Behaviors and Sleep Outcomes: Findings from the ABCD Study') published 2023 matches topic and year. Summary mentions 'Nagata, MD, assistant professor of pediatrics at the University of...' — L2 satisfied (Nagata + Sleep Health). The May 2023 EurekAlert aligns with Sleep Health 2023 publication.

EurekAlert: 'Excessive social media use linked to binge eating in US preteens...' published March 1, 2021. Topic is social media -> binge eating in preteens. Paper 24 (Nagata 2021 International Journal of Eating Disorders: 'Contemporary screen time modalities among children 9-10 years old and binge-eating disorder') published 2021 matches topic (social media/screen time -> binge eating), population (preteens), year, and author. Summary mentions 'Nagata, MD, assistant professor of pediatrics at the University of...' — L2 satisfied.

EurekAlert: 'Yes, social media might be making kids depressed' published May 21, 2025. Summary contains direct quote from Nagata: 'These findings provide evidence that social media may be contributing to the development of depressive symptoms.' This paraphrases the core finding of paper 8 (Nagata 2025 JAMA Network Open: social media -> depressive symptoms in early adolescence). L3 satisfied: outcome (depressive symptoms), exposure (social media), direction (social media causes depression), author (Nagata). Same-day release as A0088, likely same paper.

EurekAlert: 'Sleep and social media in tweens: Tips for better rest' published July 22, 2024. Topic is social media + sleep in tweens. Paper 139 (Nagata 2024 Journal of Adolescent Health: 'Bedtime Screen Use Behaviors and Sleep Outcomes in Early Adolescents: A Prospective Cohort Study') published 2024 matches year, topic (social media + sleep + tweens), and author. Summary mentions 'Jason Nagata' — L2 satisfied (Nagata + JAH context). Paper 158 (2025) is excluded by date.

exclusion_reason: out-of-corpus topic — article about parents underestimating teen social media use does not match any of the 69 candidate papers; no paper in corpus addresses parental estimation accuracy of teen SM use
evidence: EurekAlert: 'Parents underestimate teens' social media use during...' published December 17, 2021. Despite Nagata authorship, no candidate paper covers parental underestimation of teen social media use. Paper 184 (media parenting practices) is from 2025 and covers parenting strategies, not parental accuracy of estimation. None of L1-L4 criteria satisfied for any corpus paper.

EurekAlert: 'Screen time linked to bipolar and manic symptoms in U.S....' published February 20, 2025. Summary states '10- to 11-year-olds who engage heavily with social media' and mentions Nagata as associate professor of pediatrics. Paper 49 (Nagata 2025 Social Psychiatry and Psychiatric Epidemiology: 'Screen time and manic symptoms in early adolescents: prospective findings from the ABCD Study') is a direct match: screen time (including social media) -> manic/bipolar symptoms in early adolescents. L3 satisfied: outcome (manic symptoms), exposure (social media/screen time), population (10-11 year-olds = early adolescents), direction, and 2025 date.

EurekAlert: 'Study finds addictive screen use, not total...' published June 18, 2025. Summary: 'Xiao said. Though the study does not prove addictive screen use causes mental health problems—higher addiction use trajectories are linked to...' Paper 3 (Xiao 2025 JAMA: 'Addictive Screen Use Trajectories and Suicidal Behaviors, Suicidal Ideation, and Mental Health in US Youths') matches: addictive screen use trajectories, mental health outcomes, first author Xiao, JAMA 2025. L3 satisfied: addictive use (not total time), mental health outcomes, trajectory design, Weill Cornell/Xiao context.

EurekAlert: 'Addictive use of social media, not total time, associated...' published June 18, 2025. Summary: 'Yunyu Xiao, PhD, the first and lead author, assistant professor of population health science and psychiatry at Weill...' Paper 3 (Xiao 2025 JAMA, Weill Cornell Medicine): L2 satisfied — author surname Xiao + institution (Weill Cornell) + journal JAMA named in EurekAlert context. Title paraphrases the addictive SM use (not total time) finding from paper 3.

EurekAlert: 'Addictive screen use trajectories and suicidal behaviors...' published June 18, 2025. Title is nearly verbatim paper 3: 'Addictive Screen Use Trajectories and Suicidal Behaviors, Suicidal Ideation, and Mental Health in US Youths' (Xiao 2025 JAMA). Summary contains 'Yunyu Xiao, PhD, email yux4008@med.cornell.edu' — L2 and L1 criteria strongly satisfied. This is the official JAMA EurekAlert press release for paper 3.

exclusion_reason: non-ABCD cohort — article about preschool-age children's screen time and sleep quality; no ABCD paper covers preschoolers, and the Xiao mentioned is a different researcher from paper 3's Yunyu Xiao
evidence: EurekAlert: 'Too much screen time can reduce sleep quality in [preschool-age children]' published December 12, 2024. Summary mentions 'Xiao, an expert in children's socio-emotional functioning' — this is a different Xiao, not Yunyu Xiao (paper 3, suicidal behaviors) or any other ABCD corpus author. Content is about preschoolers and sleep, not matching any of the 69 ABCD candidate papers. Provisional paper 3 (Xiao 2025 JAMA, suicidal behaviors) and paper 18 (Li 2024 Advanced Science, brain development) do not cover preschoolers' sleep.

exclusion_reason: non-ABCD cohort — article about preschoolers' academic skills; ABCD Study covers ages 9-10+ and no corpus paper addresses academic skills in preschoolers
evidence: EurekAlert: 'Screen time not harmful for academic skills of preschoolers' published July 4, 2023. Preschool population and academic skills outcome do not match any of the 69 candidate papers. Paper 3 (Xiao 2025 JAMA) is about addictive screen use and suicidal behaviors in ABCD adolescents, not preschoolers' academic skills. None of L1-L4 criteria satisfied.
